questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly defines an identity provider (IdP), as introduced in Lesson 2?
options: A centralized system of record that authenticates users, holds the authoritative directory of who they are, and issues the tokens or assertions downstream apps trust instead of running their own password store
A SIEM platform that aggregates and correlates security alerts from every connected application
A VPN concentrator that encrypts traffic between a user's device and the corporate network
A physical hardware token that generates one-time passcodes for a single application
A firewall rule set that decides which network segments a user's device is allowed to reach
A backup system that stores a snapshot of every user account in case of a leaver event
questions.explain: An identity provider (IdP) — real examples include Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, and Ping Identity — is the centralized system an organization points everything else at to answer 'who is this, and are they who they claim to be.' It authenticates users, holds the authoritative directory, and issues the tokens/assertions that downstream apps trust instead of running their own password store, which is exactly what lets it function as the 'identity plane' other controls depend on.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a SIEM, which aggregates and correlates security alerts after the fact — that's monitoring work, the SOC analyst's domain from Lesson 1, not the centralized authentication and directory role an IdP plays before any app is ever reached.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of an SP-initiated SAML single sign-on flow, from Lesson 3, in the correct order.
items: The user tries to reach the app (the service provider)
The service provider redirects the user to the IdP with a SAML authentication request
The user authenticates at the IdP
The IdP returns a signed assertion to the SP's Assertion Consumer Service URL
The SP validates the assertion's signature and starts a session
questions.explain: Each step in SAML's SP-initiated flow depends on the one before it: the SP can't request authentication until the user tries to reach it, the IdP can't issue a signed assertion until the user has actually authenticated, and the SP can't start a session until it has validated that assertion's signature. Reversing any step breaks the trust chain the whole flow is built on.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 2 calls identity its own ________ — a dedicated infrastructure layer that other security controls like SSO, Conditional Access, and Zero Trust constantly query and depend on, the same way a network has a control plane.
questions.explain: The term 'identity plane' borrows from the network control-plane idea: once an organization adopts SSO, Conditional Access, and Zero Trust, all three key off the IdP's decisions, which is exactly why identity functions as a dedicated layer everything else depends on rather than just one app among many.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly states what NIST SP 800-63B's current guidance actually recommends for passwords?
options: Favor length over complexity, screen every chosen password against known-breached password lists, and only force a reset when there's real evidence of compromise — not on a fixed calendar schedule
Require a mandatory mix of uppercase, lowercase, digits, and symbols in every password, with forced rotation every 90 days
Passwords should be at least 6 characters and don't need to be screened against breach lists, since MFA alone covers that risk
Rotation must happen annually regardless of whether there's any evidence of compromise
Complexity rules should be made stricter than before, since the old rules weren't strict enough
Passwords no longer need a minimum length as long as they're changed every 30 days
questions.explain: NIST's current Digital Identity Guidelines reset the old checklist: longer passphrases beat complexity-mangled strings, every chosen password gets screened against breach lists (Entra ID password protection and Have I Been Pwned's API exist for exactly this), and forced rotation only happens when there's specific evidence of compromise, not just because a calendar date arrived.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is exactly the outdated guidance NIST replaced — forced character-mixing and calendar-based 90-day rotation pushed users toward predictable transformations like Password1! instead of genuinely stronger secrets, which is precisely why current guidance moved away from it.

questions.prompt: In a phased MFA rollout, high-privilege accounts are enrolled earlier than general staff, even though admins tend to push back the hardest. Per Lesson 6, why?
options: Privileged accounts are the ones an attacker wants most, so protecting them earlier shrinks the window of real exposure
Admin accounts are technically incapable of using the same MFA methods as general staff, so they must be handled in a separate phase
Help-desk tickets from admins are cheaper to resolve than tickets from general staff
Regulatory requirements legally mandate that privileged accounts be the very last group enrolled
questions.explain: A standing privileged account is a maximum-value target the instant it's compromised, so the rollout protects the highest-value accounts as early as possible to minimize how long that exposure window stays open — even though admins pushing back creates real friction in that phase.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about FIDO2/WebAuthn and passkeys, per Lesson 7.
options: A FIDO2 credential is cryptographically bound to the exact origin (domain) it was created for, so it simply fails to work on a convincing phishing lookalike page
The private key in a FIDO2 credential never leaves the user's device
A passkey syncs across a user's devices through a platform provider like Apple, Google, or Microsoft
SMS-based one-time codes are just as phishing-resistant as FIDO2, since both require a second factor
FIDO2 removes the human decision point that push-bombing (MFA fatigue) attacks exploit
questions.explain: FIDO2/WebAuthn replaces shared secrets with public-key cryptography: the private key never leaves the device, and the credential is bound to the exact origin it was registered for, so it fails safely against a lookalike domain. Passkeys package that for everyday users, synced via a platform credential manager. SMS codes, by contrast, can be typed into a fake page or intercepted, and both SMS and push MFA depend on a human decision an attacker can socially engineer — exactly the push-bombing weakness FIDO2 removes by making the check automatic.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a cloud-platform-issued identity for an application that's rotated automatically, with no secret value for a developer to store or copy at all, is called a ________ identity.
questions.explain: A managed identity is issued and rotated automatically by the cloud provider itself, so there's no secret value for a developer to store or copy — the platform vouches for the application directly, unlike a static API key or service account password.

questions.prompt: A support team of twelve people has accumulated twelve nearly-identical roles — 'Support-Tier1-EastRegion,' 'Support-Tier1-WestRegion,' 'Support-Tier1-Escalation' — each differing by only one or two permissions. Per Lesson 9, what RBAC failure mode is this?
options: Role explosion — every small access variation got its own dedicated role instead of being handled as a scoped exception on a shared base role
Role mining — analyzing real usage to discover the natural role groupings that already exist
A least-privilege baseline — starting each role with the minimum access its function requires
Access creep — the gradual, unintentional accumulation of access nobody actively granted
questions.explain: Role explosion is specifically the failure mode where every small variation in access spawns a new near-duplicate role instead of reusing a shared base role with a scoped, time-limited exception — producing hundreds of roles nobody can audit. Role mining is the opposite discipline (discovering real groupings from evidence), and access creep is a different problem entirely: unneeded access that lingers on an account, not an explosion of role definitions.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about attribute-based access control (ABAC), per Lesson 10.
options: An ABAC policy can evaluate user, resource, environment, and action attributes together in one decision
ABAC requires abandoning roles entirely — a resource can use ABAC or RBAC, never both
An ABAC policy is evaluated fresh at the moment of each request, so the access decision can change if the time, device compliance, or location changes
An ABAC policy is generally easier to audit than a static RBAC role assignment, since 'who can access this' is one simple list either way

A scenario like 'a doctor may read a patient record only for patients currently assigned to their care, during their active shift' is something ABAC can express as one policy, where RBAC alone would need an unreasonable number of per-doctor, per-shift roles
questions.explain: ABAC evaluates user, resource, environment, and action attributes together, fresh at request time, so the decision can shift as context changes — layering on top of (or instead of) roles rather than requiring roles to disappear. That precision is exactly what lets it express a condition like 'only this doctor's current patients, only during their shift' as one policy instead of an unreasonable number of RBAC roles. The tradeoff is that it's genuinely harder to audit than a static role assignment, not easier, because 'who can access this right now' depends on evaluating attributes that can change minute to minute.

questions.prompt: Match each PAM/JIT term from Lessons 11-12 to what it actually is.
right: Capturing every command and screen shown during a privileged session, for later review
An account holding elevated rights continuously, whether or not the privilege is actively being used
Privileged access granted only for a limited, approved window and automatically revoked when it closes
Storing privileged account passwords in an encrypted vault, checked out on demand instead of memorized or shared
questions.explain: Standing privileged access is an account that's elevated all the time, exposed as a maximum-value target even when the privilege isn't being used. Credential vaulting stores those passwords in an encrypted vault rather than memorized or shared. Session recording captures what happened during a privileged session, which vaulting alone doesn't provide. Just-in-time access replaces standing privilege entirely with a limited, automatically-revoked window — the structural fix Azure PIM implements.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 12 notes that access reviews are also called ________ campaigns — the periodic process where a manager or resource owner confirms whether existing access is still needed.
questions.explain: Access reviews, also called certification campaigns, are the periodic discipline for persistent access that isn't activated per task — a manager or resource owner looks at who currently has access and explicitly confirms whether it's still needed, with anything not confirmed getting revoked.

questions.prompt: A Microsoft Defender Attack Surface Reduction rule is identified by the GUID above. Per Lesson 14, what does this specific rule block?
options: Credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe) — the exact kind of memory access Mimikatz-style credential dumping relies on
Office applications from creating child processes like cmd.exe or powershell.exe
Execution of potentially obfuscated scripts such as heavily obfuscated PowerShell or VBScript
Win32 API calls made directly from Office macros
questions.explain: GUID 9E6C4E1F-7D60-472F-BA1A-A39EF669E4B2 is the ASR rule that blocks credential stealing from lsass.exe — exactly the kind of memory access Mimikatz-style credential dumping relies on, which is why Lesson 14 pairs it directly with the Credential Guard and LSA Protection controls in Lesson 15.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of rolling out a new GPO hardening baseline through a pilot OU, per Lesson 13, in the correct order.
items: Create a pilot OU and move a representative slice of machines into it
Link the new baseline GPO to the pilot OU
Watch gpresult output, Event Viewer, and the help desk queue during the pilot window
Re-link (or link a second time) the same GPO to the production OUs
questions.explain: A pilot OU exists specifically so a new baseline can be observed under real conditions before it reaches the whole organization: the GPO is linked to a small, representative slice first, monitored for a defined window, and only rolled out to production OUs once that pilot period passes cleanly — never the reverse order of enforcing everywhere and watching for problems afterward.

questions.prompt: Match each Windows hardening term from Lesson 15 to what it actually does.
right: The hypervisor-based technology Credential Guard relies on to create an isolated memory region separate from the main OS kernel
A process type that only allows signed, trusted code to load into its address space
Isolates NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets inside LSAIso.exe, outside lsass.exe's normal memory space
Hardens lsass.exe itself by running it as a Protected Process Light, blocking unsigned code injection
questions.explain: Credential Guard moves the actual secrets into an isolated LSAIso.exe process using Virtualization-Based Security, the hypervisor-based technology underneath it. LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) is a separate, complementary control that instead hardens lsass.exe itself by making it a Protected Process Light — a process type that only allows signed, trusted code to load — blocking the classic Mimikatz technique of injecting an unsigned DLL.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 16, running ________ /h report.html /f on a specific machine generates an HTML Resultant Set of Policy report showing exactly which GPO won each individual setting.
questions.explain: gpresult generates the Resultant Set of Policy (RSoP) report on the actual endpoint, showing which GPO won each setting — the real check that catches a precedence problem a GPMC link alone would never reveal.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 18, what attack does setting net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies to 1 specifically defend against?
options: A SYN flood denial-of-service attack, where an attacker opens huge numbers of half-finished TCP connections to exhaust the server's connection table
A SQL injection attack against a web application's database layer
Credential dumping from lsass.exe's memory space
A man-in-the-middle attack intercepting TLS-encrypted traffic
questions.explain: SYN cookies are the kernel's defense against a SYN flood: setting tcp_syncookies to 1 lets the kernel verify a connection is legitimate without holding state for it until the handshake completes, which is exactly what defeats an attacker opening huge numbers of half-finished connections to exhaust the connection table.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about CIS Benchmark Level 1 and Level 2 profiles, per Lesson 17.
options: Level 1 recommendations have little to no impact on normal functionality and CIS expects essentially every server and workstation to meet them
Level 2 recommendations are stricter 'defense in depth,' reserved for higher-security environments like systems subject to PCI DSS
CIS Benchmarks are written unilaterally by the OS vendor rather than built through community consensus
A general-purpose application server should always target Level 2, since it's 'more secure' by definition
questions.explain: Level 1 is the broad, low-impact baseline nearly every host should meet, while Level 2 is stricter defense-in-depth reserved for higher-security environments like PCI-regulated systems — choosing which profile to target is a real engineering decision, not a default to maximize blindly, and CIS Benchmarks are consensus-built by a community of practitioners, not written unilaterally by any one vendor.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of working through a CIS Benchmark with a scanner, per Lesson 17, in the correct order.
items: Pick a profile, such as Level 1 Server
Run a baseline scan and review the pass/fail report
Triage the failures — some are genuine gaps, others are intentional exceptions
Re-scan to confirm the compliance score improved
questions.explain: A benchmark scan is a repeatable loop, not a one-time checklist: pick the profile, scan to see where you stand, triage which failures are real gaps versus deliberate exceptions, remediate the real gaps, and re-scan to confirm the fix actually took — with anything still failing on purpose documented with a justification for an auditor.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 19, hosts silently diverging from their intended hardened state over time — through patches, manual fixes, or reinstalls — is called configuration ________.
questions.explain: Configuration drift is exactly this: a fleet that was fully CIS-compliant on day one can fall to 60-95% compliant six months later as patches reset configs, manual 2 a.m. fixes forget to reapply hardening, and reinstalls silently re-enable disabled modules — without anyone deliberately changing a single setting.

questions.prompt: Maria, a DBA, is terminated. Her AD account and email are disabled the same day, but a login she had directly on a reporting SQL Server — created manually by a colleague eighteen months earlier — stays active indefinitely. Per Lesson 21, why did this specific access survive her termination?
options: It was never tied to her AD account or tracked in any system that fires on a leaver event, so the automated de-provisioning pipeline had no way to know it existed
HR failed to process her termination in the HR system at all
Her manager explicitly approved keeping the SQL Server login active after her last day
SQL Server logins are technically incapable of ever being revoked once created
questions.explain: The well-integrated part of the pipeline — AD and email — worked correctly and fired the same day. The SQL Server login survived precisely because it was created manually, outside that pipeline, and never tied to her AD account, so no system had it in its inventory of 'Maria's access' to revoke when the leaver event fired. That's exactly the gap access certification campaigns exist to catch.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about toxic combinations and separation of duties, per Lesson 23.
options: Create Vendor and Approve Payment, held together by one person, is the textbook toxic combination
Neither 'Create Vendor' nor 'Approve Payment' is necessarily dangerous on its own — the risk only exists in the pairing
A toxic combination can only exist within a single application, never by combining access across two different systems
SoD has to be evaluated against a person's total access across every system, not one application's permission list in isolation
A toxic combination requires proof that fraud actually occurred before it counts as a real risk
questions.explain: Create Vendor plus Approve Payment is the canonical toxic combination precisely because neither permission is dangerous alone — only the pairing enables a complete, unreviewed fraud cycle. A real toxic combination can span two systems entirely, which is exactly why SoD has to be checked against a person's total access footprint, not one app in isolation. And as the capstone case study shows, the combination is a real risk the moment it exists — sizing that risk doesn't require proof that fraud already happened.

questions.prompt: Match each JML term from Lesson 21 to what it actually means.
right: A person's employment or engagement ends, and all their access needs to be removed
A person is hired or newly contracted and needs access provisioned for the first time
The gradual, undocumented accumulation of access a user no longer needs, usually left behind after a role change
A person changes role, team, or department, and their access needs to change to match
questions.explain: Joiners, Movers, and Leavers name the three lifecycle moments access has to change. Access creep is the specific failure that builds up quietly, usually because mover events are good at granting new access but weak at removing the old access that's no longer needed.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in an access certification campaign, the explicit act of a manager or resource owner confirming that a specific access grant is still needed is called ________.
questions.explain: Attestation is the core mechanic that makes a certification campaign work: the reviewer must explicitly mark each line as still needed or flag it for removal, and anything not attested to by the deadline is revoked automatically — the absence of a decision counts as a 'no,' not a 'yes.'

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly defines an 'exception path,' as the term is used in rolling out a security control?
options: A documented, logged, time-limited way to exclude one legitimate workflow from a control's enforcement, without disabling the control itself
A small, representative group of users or devices a control is enforced on before an org-wide rollout
A policy state that logs what a control would have done without actually enforcing it
Business pushback strong enough to force a technically correct control to be reverted entirely
Expanding enforcement to larger groups in planned waves instead of all at once
Telling affected users and the help desk about a rollout before it happens
questions.explain: An exception path is specifically a documented, logged, time-limited carve-out for one legitimate workflow a control didn't anticipate — like adding a scanner service account to a reviewed exception group — so the control itself is never disabled just because one team hit a problem.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a pilot group, a different concept from Lesson 26 — a pilot group is where a control is first enforced to test it safely, while an exception path is how you carve out one workflow from a control that's already enforced elsewhere. Confusing the pre-enforcement test group with the post-enforcement carve-out is exactly the mix-up this chapter is built to prevent.

questions.prompt: After a new MFA-enforcing Conditional Access policy ships, risky sign-in alerts drop from 47 to 9 and legacy-authentication sign-ins drop from 1,180/day to 60/day, both measured over equivalent 30-day windows against numbers recorded before rollout. Per Lesson 28, what does this evidence actually demonstrate?
options: Real evidence the policy reduced risk — because it's measured against a recorded baseline, over an equivalent time window, not just a good-looking week with nothing to compare against
Nothing meaningful, since only a rising Microsoft Secure Score counts as proof a control worked
That the control is correctly configured, which is actually what Secure Score measures, not what these numbers measure
An anecdote, since no baseline was ever established before the rollout
questions.explain: This is exactly what real evidence looks like per Lesson 28: numbers recorded before rollout as an honest baseline, compared against the same metric over an equivalent window after rollout. Secure Score is a different, complementary signal — it confirms the control is configured as expected, but it's the before/after outcome metrics, like these alert and sign-in counts, that actually tell you whether real risk went down.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about testing a security control before enforcing it, per Lesson 26.
options: Conditional Access report-only mode logs 'would succeed' or 'would fail' for every sign-in without actually blocking or challenging anyone
ASR Audit mode logs what a rule would have blocked, without actually blocking it
A pilot group is scoped after audit or report-only data already looks clean, not before
Audit mode and report-only mode both actively block or challenge the action while logging it
questions.explain: Report-only and Audit mode both exist to show what a control would do without it actually acting — logging 'would fail' or 'would block' events for review. Only once that data looks clean does the rollout move to a small pilot group, and only after that does enforcement expand further; neither mode actually blocks or challenges anything on its own.

questions.prompt: Match each control-as-code term from Lesson 25 to what it actually is.
right: Restores an exact prior GPO snapshot by its backup ID, instead of reconstructing settings from memory
The Terraform resource that defines a Conditional Access policy as versioned configuration
A second person examining a proposed control change, via its diff, before it's merged and applied
Saves a point-in-time snapshot of every setting in a GPO before a change is made
questions.explain: azuread_conditional_access_policy is the Terraform resource that turns a CA policy into a reviewable file instead of a portal click. Backup-GPO snapshots a GPO's settings before a change; Import-GPO restores that exact snapshot by its backup ID if something goes wrong. Pull request review is the second-person check applied to the diff before either kind of control change ships.

questions.prompt: In the Castellan-Thornbury merger lab, the team chooses to federate Entra ID and Okta first rather than migrating all ~40 of Thornbury's Okta-integrated apps to Entra ID immediately. Per Lesson 29, why?
options: Migrating all 40 apps and reissuing SAML certificates at once creates real outage risk for no urgent gain, while federating lets Entra ID become the surviving identity plane as each app migrates on its own schedule
Okta is technically incapable of ever being decommissioned once an organization starts using it
Federation is required by law whenever two companies with different identity providers merge
Entra ID cannot support SAML-based applications like PolicyTrack under any circumstances
questions.explain: A full day-one migration sounds cleaner but means reissuing SAML certificates and metadata for dozens of apps all at once, during the exact weeks staff are also absorbing a merger — real outage risk for no urgent gain. Federating first lets Entra ID become the surviving identity plane immediately while Okta keeps brokering Thornbury's apps until each one migrates on its own schedule, including PolicyTrack's certificate deadline and ClaimLine's vendor-contract restriction.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Dana Whitfield toxic-combination case study, per Lesson 31.
options: The Claims Adjuster and Payment Approver combination existed on Dana's account for fourteen months before being caught
It was caught because an automated separation-of-duties check was already running against the role-assignment table
The investigation found zero instances of Dana approving her own claims during the exposure window
Remediation included both revoking the extra role immediately and adding a mutual-exclusion rule to the formal RBAC role catalog
The case was closed as a confirmed instance of fraud once the combination was discovered
questions.explain: The combination survived fourteen months precisely because no SoD check existed to catch it — it was found when a human reviewer happened to notice both role names on the same certification report line. The investigation pulled fourteen months of transactions and found zero instances of self-approval, so the risk was real but no fraud actually occurred — which is why remediation had two parts: immediately revoking the Payment Approver role, and structurally adding a mutual-exclusion rule plus a nightly automated SoD check so the next combination doesn't take a year to find.

questions.prompt: Lesson 31's case study traces the Dana Whitfield toxic combination back to a gap in one specific earlier chapter's own territory. Per Lesson 32, which chapter's gap was the root cause?
options: Chapter 3 — Authorization Models at Scale, whose RBAC role catalog never encoded a mutual-exclusion rule between Claims Adjuster and Payment Approver
Chapter 1 — Identity Architecture at Enterprise Scale
Chapter 5 — Linux System Hardening Engineering
Chapter 4 — Windows System Hardening Engineering
questions.explain: Per Lesson 32's review, the root cause traces back to Chapter 3: Thornbury's RBAC role catalog had never encoded a mutual-exclusion rule between Claims Adjuster and Payment Approver, so no provisioning system or review ever flagged the pairing as invalid in the first place — exactly the authorization-design gap that let the combination exist unnoticed for fourteen months.
